claims.text: The HfNbTiVAl10 specimens have a verified multiscale hierarchical microstructure.
Grain-size distributions, phase morphology, and interface densities can be used as input features in a machine-learning model for mechanical-property prediction.
Including hierarchical microstructure descriptors will reduce Young's-modulus prediction RMSE by at least 20% relative to conventional physical or finite-element simulations.
Including hierarchical microstructure descriptors will reduce yield-strength prediction RMSE by at least 20% relative to conventional physical or finite-element simulations.
Including hierarchical microstructure descriptors will reduce fracture-property prediction RMSE by at least 20% relative to conventional physical or finite-element simulations.
The augmented machine-learning model will be approximately ten times faster computationally than conventional simulations.
The model is intended to predict behavior under tensile and fracture testing from room temperature to approximately 800 °C and at varied strain rates.
Grain size and phase distribution are important predictors of mechanical behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Encoding multiscale heterostructural details allows the model to capture dislocation interactions that affect mechanical response.
Encoding boundary and interface information allows the model to capture boundary-strengthening effects.
Encoding compositional and geometric heterostructure details allows the model to capture local phase transformations.
Dislocation interactions, boundary strengthening, and local phase transformations collectively govern the alloy's mechanical response.
The comparator is a continuum finite-element or physically based model using classical constitutive laws without hierarchical microstructure descriptors.
Substantial microstructural domain shift outside the training distribution may prevent the model from attaining the claimed accuracy gain.
New unmodeled phases or defects arising under thermomechanical loading may prevent the model from attaining the claimed accuracy gain.
Inconsistent microstructural data quality can increase predictive uncertainty.
Independent HfNbTiVAl10 specimens with characterized microstructures can be used to compare model predictions against measured modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
The accuracy claim is falsified if independent prediction errors are not at least 20% lower than those of the conventional comparator.
The efficiency claim is falsified if the model is not markedly faster than conventional simulations.
